title: Jean-Jacques Rousseau and the Social Contract: Freedom, Nature, and Moral Duty
summary: In 1762, Jean-Jacques Rousseau shook the foundations of European feudalism with his immortal declaration: 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains'.
keywords: Jean-Jacques Rousseau and the Social Contract
full_text:
In 1762, Genevan philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau published his masterpiece, Du contrat social (The Social Contract), delivering a fatal blow to the divine right of kings:

"Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains. Those who think themselves the masters of others are indeed greater slaves than they!"

Rousseau challenged the feudal order by asserting that no political authority is legitimate unless founded upon the sovereign consent of the governed:
"Sovereignty is not an inherited property of monarchs. The legitimate authority of the state derives entirely from the General Will of the citizens entering into a social compact to protect the life, liberty, and equal dignity of all. When a government becomes tyrannical, it breaks the compact, and the citizens retain the natural right to reclaim their freedom!"

Condemned by monarchs and burned by censors, Rousseau's ideas nevertheless ignited the French Revolution and provided the philosophical bedrock for modern democratic republics.
